title: Cells and their organisation II – membrane organelles, protein transport, vesicular transport, mitochondria and chloroplasts
blurb: How membrane-enclosed compartments evolved (invagination → nuclear envelope; the endosymbiont hypothesis and its evidence).
h1: Cells and their organisation II – membrane organelles, protein transport, vesicular transport, mitochondria and chloroplasts
lede: How membrane-enclosed compartments evolved (invagination → nuclear envelope; the endosymbiont hypothesis and its evidence). Rough vs smooth ER. The three ways proteins are transported (gated through nuclear pores, transmembrane via translocators, vesicular), including the nuclear pore complex, import into mitochondria and chloroplasts, SRP and the signal hypothesis. Vesicular traffic (exocytosis, endocytosis, pinocytosis; secretory, endocytic and retrieval pathways; COP I/COP II), the Golgi (cis/medial/trans), lysosomes and peroxisomes. Finally energy: entropy and the need for ATP, chemiosmotic coupling (two stages, ATP synthase), the mitochondrial and chloroplast electron-transport chains, mitochondrion and chloroplast structure, proton-motive force, and the two parts of photosynthesis.
six: Three types of protein transport; NPC; nuclear localisation signal
Signal hypothesis: SRP, translocator, signal peptidase
Exocytosis, endocytosis, pinocytosis; secretory, endocytic and retrieval pathways

questions.q: Which coat protein mediates transport from the ER to the Golgi?
questions.e: COP II = ER export; COP I = retrograde Golgi → ER. (Slides: p. 23)

questions.q: The signal-recognition particle (SRP) directs ribosomes to:
questions.e: SRP binds the ER signal sequence and docks on the SRP receptor of the rough ER. (Slides: p. 14)

questions.q: Which is NOT evidence for the endosymbiont hypothesis?
questions.answer: Organelles can be made de novo by the cell
questions.e: Organelles cannot be made de novo, only by division. (Slides: p. 5)

questions.q: Lysosomes keep an internal pH of about:
questions.e: pH 4.5–5, maintained by an H⁺ pump. (Slides: p. 28)

questions.q: Which organelle has a single membrane, no DNA, and contains catalase?
In chemiosmotic coupling, ATP synthase is driven by:
questions.answer: the flow of H⁺ down its electrochemical gradient
wrong: direct transfer of electrons to ADP
questions.e: H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase. (Slides: p. 35)

questions.q: In mitochondria, the final electron acceptor is:
questions.e: Electrons combine with O₂ to form water. (Slides: p. 36)

questions.q: In chloroplasts, the electron-transport chain and ATP synthase are located in the:
questions.e: The thylakoid membrane is the third membrane system. (Slides: p. 46)

questions.q: Uptake of liquids by vesicles is called:
Which transport type moves proteins between the cytosol and the nucleus?
questions.e: Gated transport through nuclear pores. (Slides: p. 9)

questions.q: The Nobel Prize 2013 was awarded for discoveries concerning:
questions.e: Schekman, Rothman and Südhof, vesicle traffic. (Slides: p. 21)

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.a: Mitochondria and plastids come from an aerobic and a photosynthetic bacterium phagocytosed but not digested by an early eukaryote; part of their genes moved to the nucleus.

items.n: Name evidence for the endosymbiont hypothesis.
items.a: No de novo origin (only division), own ribosomes and DNA, two different membranes, prokaryote-like metabolism and division, modern endosymbioses (Paramecium–Chlorella, Hydra–Zoochlorella).

items.n: How did the nuclear envelope evolve?
items.a: Invagination of the plasma membrane to protect DNA, ending in a double membrane.
Protein synthesis, protein sorting, N-glycosylation.
Synthesis of almost all lipids, detoxification, regulation of cytosolic Ca²⁺ (muscle contraction).

items.n: What decides where a new protein goes?
items.a: A sorting signal in its amino-acid sequence (usually at the start).
Gated (nuclear pores), transmembrane (translocators), vesicular.
The ~30 proteins forming nuclear pore complexes.

items.n: What is imported into and exported from the nucleus?
items.a: Imported: histones, polymerases, transcription regulators. Exported: almost all RNAs.
Unfolded, across both membranes at once, needing a signal sequence, driven by ATP and the membrane potential.
Recognises the ER signal sequence, binds the ribosome and chain, and docks them on the SRP receptor of the rough ER.
Cuts off the signal sequence during translocation into the ER.
Export via secretory vesicles / uptake of outside material in vesicles / uptake of liquids.

items.n: Who won the 2013 Nobel Prize for vesicle traffic?
items.a: Randy Schekman, James Rothman, Thomas Südhof.
Secretory (outward), endocytic (inward), retrieval (returns components).
COP II: ER → Golgi. COP I: Golgi → ER (retrograde) and intra-Golgi.
Cis = entry (from ER), medial = modification, trans = exit/sorting.

items.n: Which polysaccharides does the Golgi make?
items.a: Pectins and hemicellulose (plant walls), glycosaminoglycans (animal ECM).

items.n: Lysosome pH and how it is kept?
items.a: pH 4.5–5, maintained by an H⁺ pump.

items.n: How many enzyme types do lysosomes contain?
items.a: About 40 hydrolytic enzymes.
Endocytosis, phagocytosis, pinocytosis, autophagy.
Single membrane, no DNA.
Catalase and urate oxidase.
Photorespiration in leaves; converting lipids to sugars in germinating seeds.

items.n: Why do cells need constant ATP?
items.a: To maintain order against entropy (2nd law of thermodynamics).
ATP synthesis from ADP driven by an H⁺ gradient across a membrane.
1) Electron transport pumps H⁺ (gradient). 2) H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase → ATP.
O₂, forming water.

items.n: Where do chloroplast electrons come from, and where do they end?
items.a: From water (PS II); they end reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH (after PS I).

items.n: How much more efficient is ATP production with mitochondria?
items.a: About 15×.

items.n: What are cristae, and what do they contain?
items.a: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane with the ETC and ATP synthase.

items.n: What does the mitochondrial matrix contain?
items.a: mtDNA (nucleoids), ribosomes, citric acid cycle enzymes.
pH gradient + membrane potential across the inner membrane, pulling H⁺ back through ATP synthase.
About 8 (higher than the intermembrane space).

items.n: Where are the ETC and ATP synthase in chloroplasts?
items.a: In the thylakoid membrane (third membrane system).
Light reactions (PS I + II → ATP + NADPH) and dark/carbon-fixation reactions (CO₂ → carbohydrates).

items.n: Where is the H⁺ gradient formed in chloroplasts vs mitochondria?
items.a: Inside the thylakoid (large ΔpH) vs in the crista/intermembrane space (small ΔpH).
